case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.
